Sulfur hexafluoride: a small emission with a large warming effect

SF₆ is a synthetic gas made for electrical equipment, chip factories and metal casting. The world emits only about 9,770 tonnes of it a year, but each tonne warms the climate like roughly 23,500 tonnes of CO₂ would. Because almost none of it breaks down, nearly everything ever released is still in the air, and the concentration has more than tripled since 1997.

Why a few thousand tonnes matter

SF₆ is an excellent electrical insulator and does not burn or react easily. The same stability is the problem: once released it lasts for many centuries, and its 100-year warming potential is about 23,500 times that of CO₂ on the IPCC’s fifth-assessment scale, which EDGAR uses. By that measure, 9,770 tonnes in 2025 is about 230 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. Concentrations have risen every year since NOAA’s global record began in 1997, from 4.0 to 12.7 parts per trillion in June 2026, and the yearly increase has not slowed.

There are no natural sources worth counting. Nearly all of it is made by reacting sulfur with fluorine in chemical plants.

There is almost no way out either. SF₆ barely dissolves in rain or seawater and isn’t broken down by sunlight or chemistry in the lower atmosphere. The only real sink is the mesosphere, above about 60 kilometres, where molecules capture free electrons or are split by the most energetic ultraviolet light. Air takes years to circulate that high, so removal is slow. The IPCC still uses a lifetime of 3,200 years, but two 2017 studies that accounted for electron capture put it much shorter: about 850 years, from measurements of mesospheric air descending into the polar vortex (Ray and colleagues), or about 1,300 years, from a global model (Kovács and colleagues). A shorter lifetime barely changes the 100-year warming potential; it matters over millennia.

Whichever estimate is right, the sink is tiny. The roughly 330,000 tonnes now in the air lose between about 100 and 400 tonnes a year, a few percent of annual emissions. Even with the shortest lifetime, nearly 90% of what is released today will still be there a century from now. It also means the concentration record doubles as an emissions check: in 2025 the global average rose by 0.43 parts per trillion, which converts to about 11,000 tonnes of SF₆ added, more than EDGAR’s 9,770.

Where the emissions come from

Most SF₆ is not emitted when it is made. It escapes during use, mostly as slow leakage from equipment and at end of life. EDGAR splits emissions into four source categories:

Electrical equipment and other product use (92% of 2025 emissions). SF₆ insulates high-voltage switchgear and circuit breakers. It leaks over the equipment’s lifetime and when it is serviced or scrapped.
Metal industry (5%). It covers molten magnesium to stop it burning during casting. China is the world’s largest magnesium producer.
Electronics industry (3%). Semiconductor and display makers use it for etching and for cleaning process chambers.
Chemical industry (1%). This is the production of SF₆ itself. Only eight countries report emissions here: Belgium, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the US.

What the map shows

China has been the largest emitter since about 2010 (the US led before that) and accounted for about 74% of the dataset’s 2025 total, up from about 2% in 1990. India, the US, Iran, Saudi Arabia and South Korea come next. Those are places with large grids, magnesium industries or chip plants, not necessarily SF₆ factories. Where a gas is made and where it leaks are often different places.

Four estimates, two methods

Three of the datasets here count SF₆ from the bottom up. They take activity data, such as how much switchgear is installed or how much magnesium is cast, and multiply it by an assumed leak or emission rate. EDGAR does this for every country with one method. GAINS, IIASA’s emissions model, does the same with its own assumptions. The national inventories that 42 countries submitted to the UN climate convention (UNFCCC) in 2025 are those countries’ own counts, covering 1990 to 2023.

The fourth works from the top down. Martin Vojta and colleagues (2024) took SF₆ measurements from monitoring stations worldwide and ran an atmospheric transport model backward in time to work out where the gas must have been released, for 2005 to 2021. Because the inversion needs a starting guess, they ran it three times, seeded with country reports, EDGAR and GAINS. The line shows the average of the three runs and the shading shows their combined uncertainty range.

United States360–230480 (360–710)
European Union (27)200209230250 (220–290)

Three patterns stand out. First, the atmosphere sees more SF₆ than the countries in EDGAR’s file add up to: the inversion’s 2021 world total is about 30% higher, though EDGAR’s own figure has caught up to roughly that level by 2025. Second, where the inversion can check reported numbers, it finds them too low. Vojta and colleagues conclude that the US, EU and China all underestimated their emissions in their reports to the UN. For the EU, the 27 member states reported 209 tonnes for 2021, against an inversion estimate of about 250.

Third, the bottom-up estimates disagree most about China. GAINS puts China at 8,400 tonnes in 2020, nearly its entire global total, which the inversion study calls unrealistic. Excluding the run seeded with GAINS, the inversion puts China at about 5,160 tonnes in 2021, close to EDGAR. The inversion is weakest where there are few monitoring stations, which includes much of South Asia, Africa, the Middle East and South America. There its answer depends heavily on the starting guess, so the world total is better constrained than the split between those regions.

Africa, the Middle East, Latin America and Asia

The comparison above covers the places best watched by monitoring stations. Elsewhere, estimates rest mostly on bottom-up accounting, and the two models can disagree sharply. Here I group countries four ways: Africa; the Middle East, taken as the Gulf states, Iran, Iraq, the Levant and Yemen (Turkey and Egypt are left out); Latin America and the Caribbean; and Asia, taken as Central, East, South-East and South Asia, with Iran counted in the Middle East instead. China accounts for about 82% of Asia’s EDGAR total in 2021, so the table also shows Asia without it.

The models disagree most in Africa and the Middle East. EDGAR puts Africa at about 250 tonnes in 2021, roughly ten times GAINS’s figure for 2020, and the Middle East at about 480, more than six times GAINS. The gap is not about coverage. EDGAR’s file includes only six African and six Middle Eastern countries, yet its totals are still far higher, because it assigns those countries much larger emissions from electrical equipment. South Africa is about 97 tonnes in EDGAR and 7 in GAINS; Iran is 187 and 10. The inversion sides with EDGAR, putting Africa at about 300 tonnes and the Middle East at about 830.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception. EDGAR, GAINS and the inversion all land near 70 tonnes, a small share of the world total. They agree on the size but not the source: EDGAR spreads it across Venezuela, Mexico and Brazil, while GAINS puts most of it in Brazil.

Asia’s totals are mostly China’s, so they repeat the pattern from the comparison above: GAINS highest at about 8,700 tonnes, the inversion at about 7,000 and EDGAR at about 5,900. Without China the order changes. The inversion puts the rest of Asia at about 1,900 tonnes, nearly twice EDGAR’s 1,060 and seven times GAINS’s 280. Most of the difference is in South Korea (about 650 tonnes in the inversion against 240 in EDGAR), Taiwan (200 against 40) and India (530 against 430). South Korea and Taiwan lie within reach of East Asian monitoring stations, so those increases are better constrained than most in this section.

Treat the other inversion numbers with care. The grid Vojta and colleagues published comes from a single run, seeded with an earlier EDGAR version, and few monitoring stations sample air from Africa, the Middle East, South Asia or South America. Where the network is thin, the inversion stays close to its starting guess: for Africa it moved EDGAR v8’s 268 tonnes only to 303, and for Latin America and the Caribbean from 66 to 74. The larger change for the Middle East, from 476 to 833 tonnes, could partly reflect emissions from neighbouring regions that the stations can’t tell apart, and the Middle East line swings widely from year to year, between about 430 and 1,210 tonnes since 2018, another sign that the network constrains it only weakly. The authors’ own conclusion is that emissions appear to be rising in poorly monitored regions, including India, Africa and South America, and that more monitoring is needed to confirm it.

Where emissions could go

The scenarios behind the next generation of climate model runs, known as CMIP7, include SF₆. These runs will inform the IPCC’s seventh assessment. Seven integrated assessment models each produced one “marker” scenario. They range from High, where emissions keep climbing, to Very Low, where the world moves fast to cut every greenhouse gas. All seven start from 9,350 tonnes in 2023, the figure in the historical record used for CMIP7. That is about 1,000 tonnes above EDGAR’s estimate for the same year, and closer to what the atmosphere suggests.

Very Low (REMIND-MAgPIE)4,4201,930910

Five of the seven scenarios cut SF₆ emissions by more than half by 2050, and several do most of that within this decade. Medium, Medium-to-Low and Very Low all fall from about 9,400 tonnes in 2025 to under 4,500 by 2030. Nothing like that has happened yet: global emissions have risen in almost every year on record, and only the EU has shown a sustained decline. High is the exception, rising to about 12,300 tonnes by 2100. High-to-Low stays near today’s level until mid-century before falling, Medium creeps back up in the second half of the century, and Medium-to-Low briefly rebounds to about 6,300 tonnes in 2045.

One caution: SF₆ is a minor gas for these models. The dataset fills gaps in what a model reports using relationships drawn from other scenarios, a step called infilling, so the SF₆ pathways mostly reflect each scenario’s overall climate ambition rather than a detailed plan for switchgear.

What matters for the climate is how much SF₆ is in the air, and because so little is removed, cutting emissions slows the rise in concentration but doesn’t reverse it. To show this, I ran each scenario’s emissions through a simple model of the atmosphere: each year adds that year’s emissions and loses a small fraction to the mesosphere, set by the lifetime.

The concentration is still rising in 2100 in all seven scenarios. Under Very Low it reaches about 17 parts per trillion, a third above today’s level; under High, about 42, more than three times today’s. The lifetime hardly matters on this timescale: switching between 850 and 3,200 years changes the 2100 values by less than 2 parts per trillion. Even 1,000 tonnes a year keeps adding to the stock, so what is emitted this century will still be warming the next one.

How much warming SF₆ causes

SF₆’s warming effect follows its concentration. Using the IPCC’s figure for how strongly it absorbs heat (0.567 watts per square metre for each part per billion), today’s 12.7 parts per trillion trap about 0.007 watts per square metre. That is roughly 0.2% of the 3.1 watts per square metre that all human activities now add. To turn that into a temperature, I used the simple two-layer climate model the IPCC uses for its emission metrics, which warms 3 °C for a doubling of CO₂, driven by the official CMIP7 concentration series: the historical record to 2022, then each scenario.

By 2025, SF₆ had warmed the planet by about 0.003 °C, around 0.2% of the 1.37 °C of human-caused warming. That is far too small to measure directly; it is calculated from the gas’s concentration and its known heat-trapping strength. The figure is small because so few tonnes are released, not because the gas is weak. And it keeps growing: by 2100 SF₆’s contribution reaches about 0.005 °C in Very Low and 0.0115 °C in High, roughly twice to four times today’s.

The dashed line shows what would happen if all SF₆ emissions stopped in 2026. Warming would still creep up, to about 0.0035 °C by 2100, because the gas already in the air stays there and the oceans are still catching up with the heat it traps. That sets a floor under every scenario: about two-thirds of SF₆’s warming in 2100 under Very Low comes from gas already emitted by 2025.

The likely ranges reflect only uncertainty in how strongly the climate responds to added heat. They leave out uncertainty in SF₆’s heat-trapping strength and in the emissions themselves. The official CMIP7 concentrations used here agree with the simple calculation in the previous section, at its default 1,300-year lifetime, to within about half a part per trillion in 2100.

Alternatives to SF₆

The source that dominates the data, electrical equipment, is also where replacements are furthest along. This section covers switchgear only. Magnesium casting and chip making use SF₆ for different jobs and have their own substitutes, which I haven’t covered.

There are two main approaches, and they differ in one important way.

Vacuum switching with clean air. Vacuum interrupters break the current and the insulating gas is plain air (80% nitrogen, 20% oxygen), which has no warming effect. This is long established at medium voltage. Siemens Energy reports more than 1,000 clean-air switchgear units in operation, the first in a Bergen, Norway substation in 2018. The open question is high voltage. Hitachi Energy has argued in EU consultations that clean-air high-voltage substations would be over 50% larger and need far more aluminium, while other manufacturers are building clean-air equipment at higher and higher voltages.
Gas mixtures with fluoronitrile or fluoroketone. These products (GE Vernova’s g3, Hitachi Energy’s EconiQ) mix a small share of a fluorinated compound into CO₂ or oxygen. Manufacturers say they cut warming potential by about 99% compared with SF₆, in equipment of similar size. But they are still fluorinated gases. The main supplier of the fluoronitrile, 3M, announced it would stop making PFAS chemicals by the end of 2025, and the EU’s high-voltage dates apply to fluorinated gases with any warming potential of 1 or more.

Where the rules are strictest

The EU’s F-gas Regulation (2024/573) sets dates after which new switchgear using fluorinated gases cannot be put into operation. It does not force existing equipment out, and from 2035 it bans newly produced SF₆ for servicing.

FromSwitchgear
1 Jan 2026Medium voltage up to 24 kV (all fluorinated gases)
1 Jan 202852 to 145 kV
1 Jan 2030Medium voltage above 24 kV up to 52 kV
1 Jan 2032Above 145 kV

California has begun phasing out new gas-insulated equipment, and New York has adopted a similar schedule starting in 2027, according to an industry summary of those rules. I haven’t checked the state regulations themselves.

The strongest examples so far

There is no single best case. It depends on what you measure.

Highest voltage, Germany. TenneT and Hitachi Energy completed site acceptance tests of what they call the world’s first SF₆-free 420 kV gas-insulated switchgear in a transmission network.
Largest deployment push, China. State Grid has commissioned a 420 kV SF₆-free breaker at the Haishiwan substation in Gansu. It has bought Hitachi’s 145 kV equipment since 2022, and a 550 kV gas-insulated switchgear for Central China finished manufacturing and testing in January 2026. Japan’s Chubu Electric has also ordered a 550 kV unit.
Longest track record, Norway. Clean-air equipment has run there since 2018. An industry market report also credits GE Vernova with two 420 kV SF₆-free substations for Statnett and Equinor; I couldn’t confirm that from a primary source.
First adopters elsewhere. SP Energy Networks installed the UK’s first SF₆-free unit. Belgium’s grid operator Elia and Siemens Energy are developing a 420 kV clean-air design under an EU programme.

Most of these claims come from the manufacturers and their customers, so independent long-term reliability data is still thin. And because SF₆ equipment lasts for decades, leakage from the installed base will keep showing up in emissions data long after new sales switch over.

What the data can’t tell you

EDGAR estimates emissions from activity data, country reports and expert judgment; it does not measure them. The latest years are extrapolated with a fast-track method and are provisional. The file has no plant locations, so the map cannot show where SF₆ is made, only which countries report production-related emissions. Grey countries have no estimate in the selected dataset, not necessarily zero emissions.

The country reports cover only the 42 countries that filed a full inventory in 2025, mostly industrialized ones, and run to 2023. The United States did not submit in 2025, and Belarus marked its SF₆ figures as withheld under a flexibility provision. GAINS publishes its global SF₆ estimate as a 0.5° grid rather than a country table, so I summed grid cells within each country’s simplified border; small countries and border regions may be slightly misallocated. The inversion’s tables cover the world, China, the US and the EU as averages of three runs; its published grid, used for the regions and for every other country on the map, holds only the run seeded with EDGAR v8, which I summed by country in the same way.
